title: 175 Years of Direct Democracy: A Quantitative Analysis of Swiss Federal Votes
text:
1 Introduction
For most Americans, democracy is a major event that happens every two or four years. For me, it is a quarterly routine. Up to four times a year, every Swiss citizen receives an envelope from the government—not to elect a representative, but to vote directly on the laws themselves. Whether it is a constitutional amendment or a challenge to a parliamentary decision, the final word often rests with the voters.
To an outsider, this system offers a fascinating mix of direct power and complex checks and balances. We don’t just elect officials; we can challenge federal laws (referendums) and even propose our own constitutional amendments (initiatives). However, this is not simple majority rule. Much like the U.S. balances the popular vote with state representation, Switzerland often employs a “Double Majority,” requiring specific votes to win both the national popular support and a majority of the 26 cantons to pass.
Using the comprehensive Swissvotes dataset, which covers every federal vote since 1848, this project moves from anecdote to empirical analysis. I will explore the long-term patterns of this system by asking: How often do voters actually follow the government’s official recommendation? Which topics appear most frequently on the ballot? And in a system designed to balance power, how often is the will of the people actually blocked by the “Double Majority” or influenced by campaign cash?

title: 2  Data
text:
2.1 Description
This project will use the Swissvotes dataset, the definitive scholarly resource on Swiss federal referendums, which is curated and maintained by the Année Politique Suisse at the University of Bern. The data is collected continuously and updated after every voting Sunday. The dataset contains all votes from 1848 up until the latest ones in late 2025. The dataset is provided as a single, wide-format CSV or Excel file containing 700 rows of data and several hundred columns, detailing everything from vote characteristics and national outcomes to granular cantonal results and party positions. The data accounts for 681 votes. Some of these rows represent counter-proposals or tie-breaker questions, which are linked to a primary vote but counted separately in the dataset. A preliminary review confirms that missing values are coded as both full stops (.) and empty cells (““), which will be handled during data import. As the”Missing Data Analysis” section will detail, this missingness is not random but overwhelmingly systematic and historical. It is concentrated in older votes, before granular data like parliamentary vote tallies or campaign finance was consistently archived. This is a known constraint of the data, not a flaw, and it means that while core analyses can span the full 175-year period, certain research questions will be necessarily focused on the modern era. The dataset is publicly available under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. While Swissvotes provides an exhaustive list of its official sources, it does not publish its raw code or collection methodology, so this analysis relies on the accuracy of the provided data.
